title: Safety and Effects of Gildeuretinol Acetate on Retinal Atrophic Lesions in Stargardt Disease: The TEASE-1 Randomized Clinical Trial
design: Phase II multicentre double-masked placebo-controlled RCT with crossover arm plus added natural-history cases
population: Age ≥12 with clinical Stargardt disease, well-demarcated reduced autofluorescence, ≥1 disease-causing ABCA4 variant (7 US sites)
intervention: Oral gildeuretinol acetate (deuterated vitamin A) 14 mg or 24 mg daily
comparator: Placebo (24 months, or 12 months then drug) plus natural-history controls
primaryOutcome: Growth rate of well-delineated atrophic lesions on fundus autofluorescence
funding: Industry (Alkeus Pharmaceuticals; several authors are employees)
gradeWhy: Small sample, surrogate imaging endpoint, headline result relies on non-randomised natural-history controls
bottomLine: Oral deuterated vitamin A slowed Stargardt atrophy growth by about 15–22% over two years, but vision didn't differ. The effect is small, on an imaging surrogate, and the headline analysis leans on non-randomised controls. Interesting, but not practice-changing.
summary: TEASE-1 randomised 50 people with ABCA4 Stargardt disease to two doses of oral gildeuretinol or placebo for two years, then added 54 natural-history cases to the untreated group. Atrophy grew 0.182 mm/y on drug vs 0.232 mm/y untreated (21.6% relative reduction). Restricted to randomised participants only, the difference shrank to 14.9% but stayed significant. No treatment-related serious adverse events, liver problems or night-blindness were reported. Visual function benefit was not shown in the abstract.

keyResults.label: Atrophy growth (√area), drug vs untreated (placebo + NH)
Significance level used for power calculation

adds: First randomised, masked evidence that an oral visual-cycle modulator can slow Stargardt atrophy growth
Oral, daily, apparently well tolerated — no night-blindness signal, unlike other visual-cycle drugs
Prespecified randomised-only sensitivity analysis is reassuring that the effect is not purely an artefact of natural-history controls
lacks: Tiny trial: only 10 on placebo throughout (+10 crossover) — imprecise
Powered at α = 0.20, a very lenient threshold; the placebo arm was then 'augmented' with natural-history cases added during the masked review
Placebo arm was 80% male vs 30% in the drug arm — baseline imbalance
Surrogate endpoint; vision (BCVA) did not differ between groups
One case of papilloedema/raised ICP on 24 mg — a vitamin A-type effect worth watching
Trial ran 2015–2019, published 2026; sponsor-employed authors; US only

bias.note: Randomised arms fine, but primary comparator includes non-randomised natural-history cases
FAF lesion area is objective if graded centrally
Long delay to publication; functional outcomes not in abstract

practice: Do not prescribe — gildeuretinol is not licensed in the UK; this is phase II evidence
Useful for genetics/IRD clinic conversations: there are real trials of oral treatments for ABCA4 disease
Reinforce standard advice: avoid vitamin A supplements, UV protection, low-vision support
Consider signposting eligible patients to Stargardt trials via the IRD service or Retina UK

counselling.script: There's a new tablet being tested for Stargardt disease. It's a modified form of vitamin A designed so the eye doesn't build up the waste products that damage the retina. In a small two-year trial, the damaged patches at the back of the eye grew a bit more slowly in people taking it — roughly a fifth slower. That's encouraging, but we don't yet know if it actually helps people see better, and it isn't available on the NHS or licensed in the UK. Bigger trials are needed. For now, please don't take ordinary vitamin A supplements, as those may make things worse.
points: Slowed the damaged patches, not proven to protect sight

ifTheyAsk.a: Not routinely — only through a clinical trial. I can see whether you might be eligible for one.

ifTheyAsk.q: Should I take vitamin A tablets instead?
ifTheyAsk.a: No. Ordinary vitamin A supplements are thought to speed up Stargardt damage. This drug is a specially modified version.

verdictWhy: Promising signal on a surrogate in a small phase II trial with lenient statistics and borrowed controls; vision unchanged. Needs phase III with functional endpoints.

title: Avacincaptad Pegol Slows Progressive Ellipsoid Zone Degradation and Loss in Eyes with Geographic Atrophy
design: Post hoc analysis of two RCTs (GATHER1 phase II/III, GATHER2 phase III)
intervention: Intravitreal avacincaptad pegol 2 mg (complement C5 inhibitor)
primaryOutcome: Change in total and partial ellipsoid zone (EZ) attenuation on SD-OCT
funding: Industry (Astellas); some authors employed by sponsor
gradeWhy: Post hoc, OCT surrogate, 12 months only, sponsor involvement
bottomLine: Eyes with more ellipsoid-zone damage at baseline grew GA faster, and avacincaptad slowed EZ loss versus sham over a year. Useful for prognostication on OCT, but it is post hoc and does not show visual benefit.
summary: Using GATHER1 and GATHER2 OCT scans, the authors measured photoreceptor (EZ) integrity. In sham eyes, worse baseline EZ attenuation predicted faster GA growth and more EZ loss. ACP reduced growth of total EZ loss by 19.5% and partial EZ attenuation by 55.3% at 12 months versus sham. The authors propose EZ metrics to select high-risk patients.

keyResults.label: Reduction in total EZ attenuation growth vs sham
Reduction in partial EZ attenuation growth vs sham

adds: Shows EZ attenuation on OCT predicts GA growth — a practical prognostic marker
Suggests complement inhibition protects photoreceptors at the junctional zone, not just RPE
Supports OCT-based rather than FAF-only monitoring of GA
lacks: Post hoc analysis — hypothesis-generating, multiplicity not addressed in abstract
Surrogate imaging outcome only; GATHER trials did not show meaningful visual-function benefit
Only 12 months; GATHER2 eyes were not centre-involving
Proprietary segmentation software, not available in NHS clinics
Industry-funded

bias.note: Endpoints not prespecified in the parent trials
Certified reader validation of automated segmentation

practice: Avacincaptad (Izervay) is not NICE-recommended/available on the NHS — no direct prescribing impact
On OCT, comment on EZ loss beyond the atrophy margin as a sign of faster progression when counselling
Useful talking point for GA patients asking about US treatments

counselling.script: Geographic atrophy is a slow wearing-away of the light-sensing layer at the centre of the eye. In America there is an injection that slows how fast these patches grow, by roughly a fifth to a half depending on how it's measured. This new study looked closely at scans and found the injection also protected the light-sensing cells around the edge of the patches. However, people treated in these trials did not notice clearly better eyesight, and the treatment needs injections every month or two. It isn't available on the NHS at the moment.
points: Slows the patches, doesn't restore sight
Your scans can help show how quickly things are changing

ifTheyAsk.q: Can I pay for it privately?
ifTheyAsk.a: It isn't licensed in the UK at present. I'll let you know if that changes.
I can compare your scans over time and tell you how quickly it's changing.

verdictWhy: Good prognostic insight from robust trial imaging, but post hoc and the drug is unavailable in the NHS.

title: Meta-analysis of sodium glucose transport 2 inhibitors versus other glucose-lowering agents on the progression of diabetic retinopathy and diabetic macular edema
design: Systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis with meta-regression (mostly observational studies)
population: People with type 2 diabetes on SGLT2 inhibitors vs other glucose-lowering drugs
gradeWhy: Pooled observational data dominate; residual confounding likely
bottomLine: SGLT2 inhibitors were associated with about 23% lower risk of DR progression and 25% lower DME progression than other diabetes drugs. Mostly observational data, so it's an association, not proof.
summary: Pooling 16 studies with nearly 1.8 million patients, SGLT2i use was linked to lower relative risk of DR progression (RR 0.77) and DME progression (RR 0.75) versus all other glucose-lowering drugs and each subclass. The benefit was largest versus sulfonylureas. In absolute terms, with a 20% baseline progression rate the risk difference was about 4%.

keyResults.label: DR progression, SGLT2i vs all others

adds: Large, consistent signal across comparator classes
Gives absolute risk framing (≈4 fewer progressions per 100 at 20% baseline)
Fits with the cardiorenal reasons diabetologists already prefer SGLT2i
lacks: Mostly retrospective claims/cohort data — confounding by indication (healthier, newer-drug users)
DR progression definitions vary and are often coded diagnoses, not graded photos
No individual RCT designed with retinopathy as primary outcome
Two-author review; risk-of-bias methods not described in abstract

bias.note: Small author team; RoB tool not stated in abstract

practice: When writing to GPs/diabetologists about DR/DMO patients, it is reasonable to say SGLT2i are associated with lower retinopathy progression
Do not tell patients to switch medicines — glucose drug choice belongs to their diabetes team
Keep emphasising HbA1c, blood pressure and lipid control

counselling.script: Some diabetes tablets, called 'flozins' — like dapagliflozin or empagliflozin — have been linked in large studies with slightly less worsening of diabetic eye disease, roughly 4 fewer people out of 100 getting worse over time compared with other tablets. These studies watched what happened rather than testing it in a trial, so we can't be sure the tablet itself is the reason. Please don't change your medicines yourself; I can mention it in my letter to your GP or diabetes team, who'll weigh it up with your heart and kidneys in mind.
points: Linked with less eye disease progression
Not proven to be the cause
Don't change medication without your diabetes team

ifTheyAsk.q: Should I ask my GP to switch?
ifTheyAsk.a: It's worth raising, but the choice depends on your whole health. I'll note it in my letter.

verdictWhy: Consistent observational signal worth sharing with diabetes teams; not RCT-level proof.

title: Assessing the risk of diabetic retinopathy progression with GLP-1 receptor agonists: a systematic review and meta-analysis
design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs and retrospective cohorts (PROSPERO registered)
population: Adults with diabetes on GLP-1 receptor agonists
gradeWhy: Mixed RCT and cohort data, heterogeneity, imprecise semaglutide estimates
bottomLine: Overall, GLP-1 agonists were not associated with DR progression (RR 1.07, non-significant), but semaglutide stood out with a possible signal. Keep the SUSTAIN-6 warning in mind for patients with established retinopathy.
summary: Eleven studies were pooled. GLP-1RA use showed no significant association with DR progression overall (RR 1.07, 95% CI 0.90–1.28), with no differences by drug or region. Semaglutide had the highest risk estimates in two studies (RR 1.76 and 6.41, the latter very imprecise). Low risk of bias and no publication bias were reported.

keyResults.label: Pooled DR progression, GLP-1RA vs comparators

adds: Reassurance at class level for most GLP-1RAs
Highlights semaglutide as the agent to watch, consistent with SUSTAIN-6
lacks: Mixes RCTs and retrospective cohorts in one pooled estimate
Does not separate early worsening from rapid HbA1c drop from long-term effect
No stratification by baseline retinopathy severity — the key clinical question
Doesn't address NAION, which matters with semaglutide
Small number of studies for subgroup analysis

bias.note: Different drugs, comparators and DR definitions

practice: Patients starting semaglutide/tirzepatide with pre-existing moderate NPDR or worse: consider closer review in the first year
Explain early worsening from rapid HbA1c reduction is the likely mechanism
Ask about GLP-1RA use in DR clinic history-taking, including weight-loss prescriptions

counselling.script: Weight-loss and diabetes injections like Ozempic or Wegovy don't seem to make diabetic eye disease worse overall. There is one exception we keep an eye on: with semaglutide, a few studies suggest some people's eyes can get worse early on, probably because blood sugar comes down quickly. That's why, if you already have diabetic eye changes, we may see you a bit sooner after you start. Please don't stop the medicine — just tell us you're on it.
points: Tell us if you start these injections

ifTheyAsk.a: No — the benefits for your health are important. We'll just monitor your eyes a bit more closely.

verdictWhy: Reassures at class level and supports existing caution with semaglutide in established DR.

title: Subthreshold micropulse laser and conventional subthreshold laser in diabetic macular edema
design: Prospective paired-eye RCT (one eye each treatment)
population: Patients with bilateral clinically significant macular oedema (Zhongshan Ophthalmic Centre)
primaryOutcome: BCVA, CMT, choroidal thickness, FAF, microperimetry
gradeWhy: Small, short, no clear primary outcome or masking reported
bottomLine: Micropulse and conventional subthreshold laser gave similar vision and thickness outcomes at 6 months; micropulse reduced thickness a little earlier. Too small and short to change practice.
summary: Each patient's two eyes were randomised to micropulse or conventional subthreshold laser. At 6 months there was no difference in BCVA, central macular thickness, choroidal thickness, FAF changes or microperimetry. Thickness reduction became significant at month 3 with micropulse and at month 6 with conventional laser.

keyResults.label: BCVA, CMT, FAF, sensitivity at 6 months

adds: Paired-eye design controls for systemic factors like HbA1c
Adds microperimetry and FAF safety data for subthreshold approaches
lacks: Very small; not powered for equivalence — 'no difference' ≠ 'as effective'
Only 6 months
Masking and primary endpoint not described in abstract
No anti-VEGF arm — not relevant to centre-involving DME with vision loss
Paired eyes analysed as independent? Not stated
practice: Doesn't change UK pathway: anti-VEGF first line for centre-involving DMO with VA loss (NICE TA346/TA274/TA799)
Micropulse remains an option for non-centre-involving or mild DMO with good VA if your unit has the laser

counselling.script: There are two gentle types of laser for diabetic swelling at the back of the eye. A small study compared them in each patient — one type in each eye — and after six months both worked about the same for vision and swelling. One may have worked a bit faster. For most people with swelling affecting the centre, injections are still the main treatment.
points: Injections remain first choice for central swelling

ifTheyAsk.q: Can I have laser instead of injections?
ifTheyAsk.a: Sometimes, if the swelling is mild and your vision is good. It depends on your scan — let's look at it together.

verdictWhy: Underpowered, short, and doesn't address the current first-line treatment.

title: Aflibercept with and without laser therapy in diabetic macular edema: a systematic review and meta-analysis
design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs
primaryOutcome: BCVA and central macular thickness; secondary: number of injections
gradeWhy: Few small trials, imprecise estimates, unclear outcome scaling
bottomLine: Adding laser to aflibercept didn't significantly improve vision, thickness or injection numbers at 12 months. Consistent with current practice of anti-VEGF monotherapy.
summary: Six RCTs with 275 patients compared aflibercept alone versus aflibercept plus laser. At 12 months there was no significant difference in BCVA or CMT, and only a non-significant ~0.5 fewer injections with combination therapy.
adds: Pools RCT data specific to aflibercept
Supports monotherapy as the default
lacks: Only 275 patients — absence of evidence, not evidence of absence
CMT 'MD 0.13 μm' suggests standardised units were mislabelled — reporting quality concern
Laser type (focal/grid vs navigated vs micropulse) likely heterogeneous
Published in Immunotherapy, not an ophthalmology journal; first author affiliation in physics
12 months only — laser benefit, if any, may show later in reduced burden

bias.note: Small RCTs, RoB not reported in abstract

practice: Continue anti-VEGF monotherapy for centre-involving DMO; reserve focal laser for persistent focal leakage from microaneurysms
Don't cite this as strong evidence — DRCR Protocol I is still the key reference

counselling.script: For diabetic swelling at the centre of the eye, the injections do most of the work. Studies comparing injections alone with injections plus laser found the laser didn't add much — vision and swelling were about the same, and people didn't need noticeably fewer injections in the first year. So we usually start with injections alone and keep laser for particular spots that keep leaking.
points: Laser kept for specific leaking spots

ifTheyAsk.a: Perhaps slightly, but the studies didn't show a clear difference.

verdictWhy: Confirms existing practice, though the review itself is weak.

title: Cost-Effectiveness of Photobiomodulation for Intermediate Dry Age-Related Macular Degeneration: A Model-Based Analysis Using the LIGHTSITE III 24-Month Trial
design: Markov model cost-effectiveness analysis based on one RCT (LIGHTSITE III)
population: Modelled cohort with bilateral intermediate dry AMD, BCVA 20/32–20/100
n: Modelled cohort (trial data from LIGHTSITE III)
gradeWhy: Modelled outcomes resting on a single, unreplicated trial result
bottomLine: The US model says PBM costs ~$74,000 per QALY — but it hinges on LIGHTSITE III's 72% reduction in new GA, which has not been independently replicated. This is an economic model, not new clinical evidence.
summary: A 5-state Markov model with 6-month cycles over 10 years used LIGHTSITE III outcomes and AREDS natural history. PBM gained QALYs at an incremental cost of $29,556, an ICER of $73,910/QALY. Results were sensitive to device cost and to the size of GA reduction. The authors call for independent replication.

keyResults.label: Driver: relative reduction in incident GA

adds: First economic model of PBM using 24-month trial data
Transparent about the key assumption (GA reduction)
lacks: Entire result rests on one industry-sponsored trial's secondary finding
US costs and thresholds; irrelevant to NICE's £20–30k/QALY framework
Utilities derived by mapping, not measured EQ-5D
Model-based evidence sits at the bottom of the hierarchy for efficacy

bias.note: Single unreplicated trial drives the model
Sensitivity analyses done, but structural uncertainty remains

practice: PBM is not NICE-recommended for dry AMD (NICE IPG on PBM restricts it to research/special arrangements) — check current guidance before advising
Patients asking about private Valeda: explain evidence is from one trial and benefits are uncertain

counselling.script: Light therapy for dry macular degeneration is offered privately in some places. One trial suggested it might slow the development of the late 'thinning' stage, but that hasn't yet been confirmed by independent researchers. This new paper only worked out whether it would be value for money in America, assuming that one trial was right. So it doesn't add new proof that it works. It isn't available on the NHS.
points: Diet, not smoking and AREDS2-type vitamins remain the proven steps

ifTheyAsk.a: I wouldn't recommend spending money on it yet — the evidence isn't strong enough.

verdictWhy: Economic model built on an unreplicated result; no new clinical evidence and US-specific.

title: Outcomes of Complex Retinal Detachment Repair with Proliferative Vitreoretinopathy Grade C using the Cincinnati Methotrexate Protocol
design: Retrospective non-randomised comparative cohort, single tertiary centre
population: Eyes undergoing vitrectomy for RD with PVR grade C, 2019–2025
intervention: Methotrexate 40 mg/500 mL in infusion during PPV + intravitreal MTX 200–400 μg at weeks 1, 3, 6, 10
primaryOutcome: Single-surgery success, postoperative PVR, VA, final attachment
gradeWhy: Retrospective, non-randomised, likely era and surgeon effects
bottomLine: Eyes given the Cincinnati methotrexate protocol had five-fold higher odds of single-surgery success and far less recurrent PVR. Striking, but retrospective — wait for GUARD and other RCT data before adopting.
summary: In 300 eyes with PVR-C detachments, MTX-treated eyes had OR 5.15 for single-surgery success and OR 0.15 for postoperative PVR, robust to multivariable adjustment. Vision was better at 1, 3, 6 and 12 months. No difference in serious ocular adverse events was reported.
adds: Large comparative dataset for a specific, reproducible MTX protocol
Effect size is big and consistent across endpoints
Safety data for repeated intravitreal MTX
lacks: Not randomised — comparison cohort may differ (era, surgeon, case selection)
Single centre; unmasked outcome assessment
Effect sizes this large in observational data often shrink in RCTs
Corneal epitheliopathy and other MTX toxicities not detailed in abstract

bias.note: How comparison eyes were chosen is unclear
Unmasked, but outcomes are fairly objective

practice: Relevant to VR colleagues rather than MR clinic
Be aware MTX is used off-label for PVR; check local VR protocol
When counselling RD patients about re-operation risk, PVR prevention is an active research area

counselling.script: Sometimes after retinal detachment surgery, scar tissue forms and pulls the retina off again. One hospital in America has been using a drug called methotrexate inside the eye to reduce this. In their records, people given it were much more likely to need only one operation. That's encouraging, but it wasn't a proper trial, so we can't be sure yet. Your surgeon will discuss whether it's used here.

ifTheyAsk.a: That depends on your surgeon and local practice. It's worth asking them.

verdictWhy: Large effect but high risk of confounding; needs RCT confirmation.

title: Clinical outcomes of epiretinal membrane surgery in patients with good baseline visual acuity
design: Retrospective multicentre case series (4 UK centres)
population: Symptomatic ERM with BCVA 20/40 (logMAR 0.3) or better
bottomLine: In UK patients with good-vision symptomatic ERM, 80% kept or improved their vision, 92% felt better, and about 1 in 100 had major vision loss. Directly useful numbers for consent.
summary: Across four UK centres, 163 eyes with symptomatic ERM and BCVA 20/40 or better had vitrectomy and peel. Mean BCVA did not change, but 80% maintained or improved, 92% reported symptom improvement and 1.2% had a final BCVA worse than 20/200.
adds: UK, multicentre real-world consent figures for a common dilemma
Captures patient-reported symptom benefit, not just acuity
lacks: No control group of observed patients
Retrospective case notes — complications may be under-recorded
Symptom improvement not measured with a validated metamorphopsia tool
Only 12 months; cataract progression in phakic eyes not quantified in abstract

bias.note: Surgical cases only; no untreated comparator

practice: Use these numbers when referring/consenting good-VA ERM patients: ~8 in 10 stay same or better, ~1 in 100 serious loss
Distortion, not acuity, should drive the decision in this group
Remind phakic patients that cataract is likely after vitrectomy

counselling.script: The membrane on your retina is causing distortion, even though your reading vision is still good. In UK hospitals, about 9 out of 10 people with good vision who had this operation felt their symptoms improved, and 8 out of 10 kept or improved their sharpness of vision. About 1 in 100 had a serious loss of vision. If you still have your natural lens, a cataract is very likely to develop afterwards. The choice is yours — it depends on how much the distortion bothers you.

ifTheyAsk.a: Many membranes stay stable. Waiting is safe — we can monitor and operate later if it worsens.

verdictWhy: Low-level evidence but practical, UK-specific consent numbers.

title: Personalised ILM peeling for Myopic traction maculopathy
intervention: ILM peeling only within the OCT-mapped schisis area
primaryOutcome: VA, retinal thickness, schisis height, visual field
bottomLine: A tailored, OCT-guided partial ILM peel for myopic schisis gave no recurrences or complications in 10 eyes. Interesting technique, far too small to judge.
summary: The authors mapped the schisis on OCT and peeled ILM only over that zone in 10 eyes. Over more than 24 months there were no recurrences or complications, with improved VA and reduced schisis height.
adds: Describes a reproducible OCT-mapping approach to limit peel area
Rationale to protect fragile myopic nerve fibres
lacks: 10 eyes, no control (e.g. fovea-sparing or full peel)
Natural history of S2–S3 schisis is variable
Visual field benefit asserted, not shown in abstract
practice: VR technique — no change to MR clinic practice
Know that fovea-sparing / tailored ILM peel exists when discussing referral for myopic traction maculopathy

counselling.script: In very short-sighted eyes, the retina can split into layers. Surgeons are trying gentler operations that peel only the affected area. A small study of ten eyes did well with no complications, but that's too few to be sure it's better than standard surgery.

verdictWhy: Technique note; insufficient for clinical decisions.

title: Comparative Efficacy and Safety of Systemic Immunomodulatory Therapies for Non-Infectious Uveitis: A Systematic Review With Pairwise and Network Meta-Analyses
design: Systematic review with pairwise and frequentist network meta-analysis
gradeWhy: Adalimumab efficacy driven by VISUAL I/II RCTs; other comparisons sparse
bottomLine: Adalimumab is the only agent with consistent RCT evidence of reducing treatment failure in NIU (RR 0.67). Comparisons with other drugs are too sparse to rank them.
summary: Pooling 7 studies (992 participants), adalimumab reduced treatment failure versus placebo (RR 0.67, low heterogeneity) at the cost of more injection-site reactions. Mortality was inconclusive (3 deaths on adalimumab, none on placebo). The network found no clear safety differences; an infliximab urinary infection signal rested on sparse events.
adds: Confirms adalimumab's evidence base in a pooled, network framework
Highlights how thin head-to-head evidence is for other agents
lacks: Only 7 studies — network is sparse; ranking not meaningful
Conventional agents (methotrexate, mycophenolate) poorly represented; FAST trial context needed
One non-randomised study included in a network
No paediatric/JIA separation in abstract
practice: Supports adalimumab as the evidence-based biologic for NIU (NICE TA460: active non-infectious intermediate, posterior or panuveitis with inadequate response/intolerance to steroids)
Biologics are uveitis-service/rheumatology decisions — refer appropriately
Counsel about injection-site reactions

counselling.script: For long-lasting inflammation inside the eye that isn't caused by infection, the medicine with the best evidence is adalimumab, an injection you give yourself every two weeks. In trials, it cut the chance of the inflammation flaring or failing to settle by about a third. Sore or red skin where you inject is common. Other medicines are also used, but they've been compared head-to-head much less.

ifTheyAsk.a: It's widely used. It can raise infection risk, so you'll be screened for TB and other infections first and monitored.

verdictWhy: Confirms the current NICE-endorsed biologic choice.

title: Biologic Switching Strategies for Anti-Tumor Necrosis Factor Alpha Refractory Noninfectious Uveitis: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Clinical Approach
design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of mostly case reports/series plus 7 comparative studies (PROSPERO registered)
intervention: Switching biologic: intraclass (another anti-TNF) or interclass (e.g. tocilizumab, other classes)
gradeWhy: Authors' own GRADE low; built mostly on case series
bottomLine: After anti-TNF failure, switching works in most patients (83% response); switching to a different class (e.g. IL-6 blockade) did somewhat better than another anti-TNF (85% vs 71% in sensitivity analysis). Low-certainty evidence.
summary: Across 466 patients pooled from 89 studies, the overall response after switching was 83%. Interclass switching responded 89% vs 77% for intraclass (P = 0.10), becoming significant in sensitivity analysis (85% vs 71%, P = 0.044). Certainty was low.
adds: Best available synthesis on a common, evidence-poor decision
Supports considering a different mechanism (e.g. tocilizumab) after primary anti-TNF failure
lacks: 129 of 136 studies are case reports/series — strong publication bias towards responders
'Response' definitions vary
Doesn't separate primary non-response from secondary loss of response or anti-drug antibodies
No cost or NHS commissioning angle

bias.note: Successful switches more likely to be reported

practice: When anti-TNF fails, check adherence and drug levels/antibodies first
For true mechanism failure, an interclass switch (tocilizumab via NHS England commissioning) is reasonable
Discuss at uveitis MDT

counselling.script: Your current biologic hasn't fully controlled the inflammation. The good news is that most people — around 8 in 10 — do respond when switched to another medicine. Reports suggest switching to a medicine that works in a different way may work a bit better than swapping to a similar one. The evidence is mostly from individual reports, so we'll decide together with the uveitis team.
points: Most people respond to a switch
Different-mechanism drug may be slightly better

verdictWhy: Useful low-certainty guidance where no RCTs exist.

title: Comparison of the Risk of Acute Anterior Uveitis Flare Between Adalimumab and Subcutaneous Infliximab in Patients with Radiographic Axial Spondyloarthritis and Prior Acute Anterior Uveitis: A Randomized Controlled Trial
population: Radiographic axial SpA with AAU in the previous 2 years
intervention: Subcutaneous infliximab (IV induction then 120 mg SC every 2 weeks)
bottomLine: Only one flare occurred in each arm, so the trial cannot tell whether SC infliximab and adalimumab differ (HR 0.50, 95% CI 0.03–9.8). Both kept AAU quiet in almost everyone.
summary: 56 patients with axSpA and recent AAU were randomised to adalimumab or SC infliximab for 48 weeks. Each arm had one AAU flare; no differences in BCVA, axSpA activity or safety.
adds: First head-to-head randomised data for SC infliximab in AAU prevention
Both monoclonal anti-TNFs give very low flare rates
lacks: Hopelessly underpowered for the primary outcome — 'no difference' is meaningless
Open-label; flare assessment may be biased
48 weeks short for a recurrent condition
Korean population; HLA-B27 status not reported in abstract
practice: For axSpA patients with recurrent AAU, flag to rheumatology that monoclonal anti-TNFs (not etanercept) are preferred
SC infliximab appears a reasonable alternative, but evidence is weak

counselling.script: If you have recurring eye inflammation with your back condition, some of the injections your rheumatologist uses also protect the eye. In a small trial, both adalimumab and an under-the-skin version of infliximab kept flare-ups very rare — only one person in each group had one in a year. So either is reasonable; the trial was too small to say one is better.
points: Too small to pick a winner

ifTheyAsk.q: Will my etanercept protect my eyes?
ifTheyAsk.a: Etanercept is less effective for the eye. It's worth discussing with your rheumatologist if you keep having flares.

verdictWhy: Underpowered; cannot inform choice between agents.

title: Association between immune checkpoint inhibitors and the risk and prognosis of uveitis: a meta-analysis
design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of cohort studies (PROSPERO registered)
population: Cancer patients on immune checkpoint inhibitors
primaryOutcome: Uveitis risk; overall survival with ICI uveitis
gradeWhy: Few observational studies; survival analysis very low certainty
bottomLine: Checkpoint inhibitors roughly double the risk of uveitis (HR 2.26). Whether ICI uveitis predicts better cancer survival remains unknown.
summary: Five cohort studies with almost 278,000 people showed ICI therapy was associated with a higher uveitis risk (HR 2.26). Two studies on survival found no significant association (HR 0.69), with very low certainty.

keyResults.label: Overall survival in ICI uveitis (2 studies)

adds: Quantifies ICI-associated uveitis risk across large cohorts
Useful for oncology liaison and patient warning
lacks: Only 5 studies; uveitis often identified from codes
No breakdown by agent, cancer type or uveitis subtype
Absolute risk not given — uveitis remains rare
practice: Ask about immunotherapy in every new uveitis history — and about melanoma (MEK inhibitors also cause retinopathy)
Coordinate steroid treatment with oncology; most ICI uveitis responds to topical/local steroid
Consider VKH-like and anterior presentations

counselling.script: Your cancer immunotherapy works by boosting your immune system, and occasionally that boosted immune system attacks the eye, causing inflammation. Large studies show it roughly doubles the chance of this, though it's still uncommon. It usually settles with steroid drops or injections, and we'll work with your cancer team so your treatment can continue where possible.

ifTheyAsk.q: Does this mean my cancer treatment is working?
ifTheyAsk.a: Some people wonder that; the studies so far can't say either way.

verdictWhy: Confirms a clinically important association; prognostic question open.

title: Epidemiological characterization of uveitis in the elderly population: a systematic review and meta-analysis
design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of proportions (cohort and cross-sectional studies)
bottomLine: In over-60s, ~41% of uveitis is idiopathic, with herpes (~11%) the leading identified cause, then HLA-B27, sarcoid and TB (~5–6% each). Keep masquerade (lymphoma) in mind — the abstract doesn't report it.
summary: Sixteen studies were pooled. Idiopathic uveitis made up 41.5%, herpetic 11.4%, HLA-B27 6.1%, sarcoidosis 5.2%, TB 5.1% and CMV 3.1%. Heterogeneity was high, largely geographic.
adds: Pretest probabilities to tailor work-up in older patients
Highlights herpetic disease as the leading identifiable cause
lacks: Masquerade syndromes (vitreoretinal lymphoma) not reported in abstract — critical in this age group
Mostly Asian data; UK generalisability limited
Diagnostic work-up varied, so 'idiopathic' depends on how hard people looked
practice: Older patient with uveitis: always consider herpetic aetiology (check IOP, sectoral iris atrophy, corneal sensation)
Low threshold for vitreous biopsy / lymphoma work-up in older patients with vitritis
Screen syphilis and TB as standard

counselling.script: In people over 60, eye inflammation often has no single cause we can find — that's true for around 4 in 10 people. When we do find a cause, the cold-sore and shingles virus family is the most common. We'll do some blood tests to look for infections and other causes, because that changes the treatment.

verdictWhy: Useful pretest probabilities with important caveats.
